After the American Civil War ended in 1865, slavery was abolished in the United States. However, southern states introduced Jim Crow laws that enforced the separation of Black and white people in schools, transport, restaurants, public toilets and other spaces. Black voters faced literacy tests, poll taxes and intimidation at the ballot box. Segregation told Black citizens they were considered inferior, even though they were legally citizens with rights.

Civil rights campaigners challenged segregation using many methods. In 1954, the Supreme Court ruled in Brown v Board of Education that segregated public schools were unconstitutional. This was a major legal victory, but many white officials resisted and schools remained segregated in practice for years. In 1955, Rosa Parks was arrested in Montgomery, Alabama for refusing to give up her bus seat. Local activists, who were ready to organise, launched a bus boycott. For over a year, Black residents walked, shared cars and organised lifts rather than use segregated buses. The boycott worked partly because Black passengers made up a large proportion of the bus company's income.

Martin Luther King Jr became nationally known during the boycott. He argued for non-violent protest — a carefully planned, active and sometimes dangerous approach that trained participants to respond calmly to hostility. In 1963, over 200,000 people marched on Washington where King delivered his famous speech. The following year, the Civil Rights Act of 1964 banned segregation in public places and prohibited employment discrimination.

However, important roles were played by many people beyond famous leaders. Ella Baker, Jo Ann Robinson, Diane Nash and thousands of local organisers, students and church members made campaigns possible. Without grassroots action, legal victories and media attention, change would not have happened.

questions.question: What did Jim Crow laws enforce in the southern United States?
options: Equal rights for Black and white citizens
The separation of Black and white people in public spaces
Free voting rights for all citizens
Higher wages for Black workers
questions.modelAnswer: Jim Crow laws enforced racial segregation — the separation of Black and white people in schools, transport and other public spaces.

questions.question: Why was the Montgomery Bus Boycott economically effective?
options: Because the government subsidised the boycotters
Because Black passengers made up a large proportion of the bus company's income
Because the bus company was already losing money
Because the boycott only lasted one day
questions.modelAnswer: The boycott was economically effective because Black passengers made up a large proportion of the bus company's income, so refusing to use the buses hurt the company financially.

questions.question: Why did the Brown v Board ruling not immediately end school segregation?
options: Because the Supreme Court reversed the decision the following year
Because many white officials resisted and schools stayed segregated in practice
Because the ruling only applied to colleges, not schools
Because Black families refused to enrol their children in mixed schools
questions.modelAnswer: Although Brown v Board declared segregated schools unconstitutional, many white officials resisted and schools remained segregated in practice for years, showing that legal victories alone do not always change everyday life.

questions.question: What does the passage suggest about why it is important to study grassroots activists and not only famous leaders?
options: Famous leaders had no influence on civil rights campaigns
Without local organisers, students and community members, campaigns could not have functioned
Grassroots activists were better speakers than Martin Luther King Jr
Leaders deliberately stopped grassroots workers from getting recognition
questions.modelAnswer: The passage argues that without grassroots action from people like Ella Baker and Jo Ann Robinson — and thousands of unnamed local organisers — legal victories and national campaigns would not have been possible.

Apartheid was a system of racial segregation and white minority rule introduced as official government policy in South Africa in 1948. Under apartheid, Black South Africans and other non-white groups were denied equal rights. They could not vote in national elections. Their movements were restricted by pass laws. They were forced into poorly funded schools, separate hospitals and designated residential areas. Violence and imprisonment were used against those who challenged the system.

The struggle against apartheid took many forms. Inside South Africa, individuals and organisations organised protests, strikes, underground activities and political campaigns. The African National Congress was one of the most important anti-apartheid organisations. International campaigners joined in. In Britain, people boycotted South African goods, protested against South African sports teams touring the country and pressured politicians to impose economic sanctions.

Nelson Mandela became one of the most well-known figures of the struggle. He was imprisoned in 1964 and spent 27 years in jail before being released in 1990. His imprisonment became a focus for international attention and campaigning. His dignity and commitment helped make him a symbol recognised worldwide.

Apartheid did not end because of one person or one action. It collapsed through a combination of internal resistance, international economic pressure and sanctions, sporting bans that isolated South Africa globally, and eventually negotiations between the apartheid government and anti-apartheid leaders. In 1994, South Africa held its first fully democratic elections. Nelson Mandela was elected president. Apartheid's fall is a reminder that change can require sustained effort across many years and many forms of pressure.

questions.question: How did British people campaign against apartheid?
options: By sending troops to South Africa
By boycotting South African goods and protesting against sporting tours
By passing laws to abolish apartheid directly
By moving to South Africa to support protesters

questions.question: Why did Nelson Mandela become an important international symbol of the anti-apartheid struggle?

Because he negotiated apartheid's introduction personally

questions.question: What does the passage suggest about how apartheid ended, and why is this historically significant?

It ended only through military force from other countries

data.sourceTitle: Protest and Social Change in 20th-Century Britain
data.targetTitle: Protest and Social Change in 20th-Century Britain
data.sourcePassage:
Britain did not have the same legally enforced Jim Crow system as the southern United States, but discrimination was widespread and damaging. After 1945, people from the Caribbean, South Asia and other parts of the Commonwealth arrived in Britain to work and build new lives. They worked in hospitals, on buses, in factories and across public services. Many, however, faced discrimination in housing, employment, pubs and clubs. The common sign 'No Blacks, No Irish, No Dogs' on boarding houses showed how open prejudice could be.

In Bristol in 1963, campaigners organised a boycott of the city's buses after the bus company refused to employ Black and Asian workers as drivers or conductors. Organisers including Paul Stephenson used protest, media coverage and community pressure to challenge the colour bar. The bus company eventually backed down. The Bristol Bus Boycott showed that organised protest could succeed in Britain, and it helped build momentum for the Race Relations Act of 1965.

Women also campaigned for equal rights in this period. In 1968, women sewing machinists at Ford's Dagenham factory went on strike. They argued that their skilled work was undervalued because they were women. Their action attracted national attention and contributed to the Equal Pay Act of 1970.

Protests for different rights continued across the twentieth century. Disability rights campaigns challenged buildings, employers and laws that excluded disabled people from public life. LGBTQ+ campaigns challenged laws and attitudes. The Equality Act of 2010 brought many protections together under a single framework. However, legislation and real equality are not the same thing. Campaigners continued to work long after laws were passed because changing attitudes and everyday practices takes longer than changing the law.

questions.question: What was the colour bar that the Bristol Bus Boycott challenged?
options: A law requiring buses to be painted in two colours
A policy preventing Black and Asian workers from being employed as bus drivers or conductors
A rule requiring segregated seating on buses
A tax on bus fares for non-white passengers
questions.modelAnswer: The colour bar was the bus company's policy of refusing to employ Black and Asian workers as bus drivers or conductors.

questions.question: What did the Ford Dagenham sewing machinists' strike of 1968 demand?
options: Better working conditions in the factory
Recognition that their skilled work was undervalued because they were women
Higher production targets to earn bonuses
The right to join a trade union
questions.modelAnswer: The Ford Dagenham machinists argued that their skilled work was undervalued because they were women, and their strike contributed to the Equal Pay Act of 1970.

questions.question: How was discrimination in Britain different from the Jim Crow system in the United States?
options: Britain had no discrimination at all after 1945
British discrimination was mostly legally enforced through government acts
British discrimination was often informal and local rather than written into state laws, though still widespread and damaging
The United States had no discrimination because of the Civil War
questions.modelAnswer: In Britain, discrimination was often informal — in hiring, housing, pubs and clubs — rather than formally written into state law, though it was still widespread and seriously damaging.

questions.question: Why does the passage argue that passing a law does not automatically create equality?
options: Because laws in Britain were never obeyed
Because changing everyday attitudes and practices takes longer than changing the law
Because the Equality Act 2010 was immediately repealed
Because discrimination was legal in Britain until 2020
questions.modelAnswer: The passage argues that legislation and real equality are different things. Changing the law is only a first step because attitudes, habits and practices in everyday life can persist long after a law is passed.
